---
title: "quarto-index id-collision probe"
from: markdown-smart
filters:
  - index
---

# Names the document has already taken

Generated ids step over any name the document itself uses, however that name
was written. This document claims five, in the five spellings the extension
reads: a Pandoc attribute, and raw HTML with a double-quoted, an unquoted and
an uppercase-`ID=` attribute, plus a raw *inline* one — the extension reads raw
inlines as well as raw blocks, and single quotes as well as double.

One term is marked here: [zeta]{.index}. Another, twice: [eta]{.index}, and
[eta]{.index}.

::: {#qi-index}
A div claiming the generated section's own id, written as a Pandoc attribute.
Deliberately not a heading: Quarto moves a heading's id onto the section
wrapper it builds, which would put the claim somewhere the author did not
write it.
:::

```{=html}
<p id="qi-index-1">Raw HTML, double-quoted.</p>
<p id=qi-index-2>Raw HTML, unquoted.</p>
<p ID="qi-index-3">Raw HTML, uppercase attribute name.</p>
```

A raw inline claims the fifth: `<span id='qi-index-4'>single-quoted</span>`{=html}.

::: {.qi-index-here}
:::

# Names a mark and another element both claim

An id the author wrote on a mark is the mark's link target, and an id written
anywhere else on the page belongs to whatever the author wrote it on. Where the
two are the same name, the mark is the one that yields: the extension writes
only its own spans, so it anchors the mark on a minted id, reports the refusal,
and the other element keeps the name it was given. One mark per spelling the id
census reads, so a claim written in raw HTML weighs exactly as a Pandoc
attribute does.

A Pandoc attribute claims one: [alpha]{#shared-attr .index}.

::: {#shared-attr}
A div claiming the name the alpha mark was written with.
:::

Raw HTML claims three more: [beta]{#shared-dq .index}, [gamma]{#shared-uq
.index} and [delta]{#shared-up .index}.

```{=html}
<p id="shared-dq">Raw HTML, double-quoted.</p>
<p id=shared-uq>Raw HTML, unquoted.</p>
<p ID="shared-up">Raw HTML, uppercase attribute name.</p>
```

A raw inline claims the fifth: [epsilon]{#shared-sq .index} against
`<span id='shared-sq'>single-quoted</span>`{=html}.

A sixth is a name the numbering would otherwise mint, so a claim on one of
those is refused exactly as any other claim is rather than being handed over by
the mint: [theta]{#qi-mark-3 .index}.

```{=html}
<p id="qi-mark-3">Raw HTML claiming a name the numbering mints.</p>
```

# Two marks written with one name

Neither mark is anything but a mark, so document order settles which keeps the
name: [kappa]{#twin .index} comes first and keeps it, and [lambda]{#twin
.index} yields.

# Names nothing contests

A mark whose id no other element carries keeps it, whatever the name is. Three
here: one nobody else wrote, [mu]{#solo .index}; one in the heading below,
which is where an anchor cannot sit, so the id moves to an empty span just
after it; and one spelled as a name the numbering would otherwise mint,
[xi]{#qi-mark-9 .index}, which the numbering steps over as it always has.

## A heading carrying [nu]{#in-heading .index}

Text under that heading, so the section is not empty.

# Names only a comment carries

An HTML comment is not part of the rendered page: an id written inside one is
on nothing a link can reach, so it contests nothing and a mark keeps the name
it was written with. Two here, one per shape a comment arrives in — a comment
written on its own, and one inside a raw HTML block: [omicron]{#in-comment
.index}, and [pi]{#in-raw-comment .index}.

<!-- An earlier draft of this paragraph: <p id="in-comment">gone</p>. -->

```{=html}
<p id="kept-alive">Raw HTML beside a comment.</p>
<!-- <p id="in-raw-comment">also gone</p> -->
```

The links an author writes to those marks still resolve: [to omicron](#in-comment)
and [to pi](#in-raw-comment).

# Cross-references and a name something else claims

A mark that only points at another entry files no locator, so nothing the index
writes links to it. It carries an id all the same, and one id still names one
element: where something else on the page claims that name, the mark yields it
and says so. No locator moves, there having been none.

A `see=` mark against a div claiming its name: [rho]{#xref-dup .index see="mu"}.

::: {#xref-dup}
A div claiming the name the rho mark was written with.
:::

A `see-also=` mark against raw HTML claiming its name: [sigma]{#xref-raw .index
see-also="mu"}.

```{=html}
<p id="xref-raw">Raw HTML claiming the name the sigma mark was written with.</p>
```

A cross-reference mark whose name nothing else claims keeps it, and nothing is
reported: [upsilon]{#xref-solo .index see="mu"}.

## A heading carrying [tau]{#xref-heading .index see="mu"}

A cross-reference mark written in a heading, whose id Quarto would otherwise
copy into the table of contents. The name is claimed below as well, so this
mark yields it where the relocated anchor lands.

::: {#xref-heading}
A div claiming the name the tau mark was written with.
:::

# A cross-reference and a locator mark written with one name

Where two marks share a name and one of them files a locator, the locator mark
keeps it whichever is written first: a reader follows the locator, and nothing
the index writes points at a cross-reference. The cross-reference comes first
here and yields anyway: [phi]{#twin-xref .index see="mu"}, then
[chi]{#twin-xref .index}.
